newsitem.title: JAPAN: ASIAN TRADERS SEE LME ALUMINIUM TRYING RESISTANCE.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN TRADERS SEE LME ALUMINIUM TRYING RESISTANCE.

text.p: Aluminium on the London Metal Exchange (LME) looks set to attack the next resistance at $1,750, though a small correction may be in store given the speed of its latest rally, Asian traders said on Thursday.
"They'll try to break the major resistance at $1,750 (per tonne)," said a trader at a European trade house.
"If they can successfully bring it above $1,750, there might be some more stop-loss buying."
By 0510 GMT, three-month aluminium was quoted at $1,747/$1,751, up from $1,742/$1,745 at 1800 GMT on Wednesday and the kerb close of $1,741.5
Traders said the metal might see another correction towards $1,700 when London opens for trade on Thursday. It touched a low of $1,712 on Wednesday before scoring a gain of $20.5.
Once the next resistance at $1,750 is broken, it could advance towards $1,900 in the short term, as the latest rally was forcing many users to rethink their strategy, they said.

"A lot of consumers are not really hedged in the forwards. They were only buying from hands to mouth," one trader said. "Now the market has started to rally, they might have to rethink their strategy."

The trader added: "In terms of Japanese users, they should have taken the chance when the dollar was around 110 yen. Now the yen is weaker. The price of aluminium seems to be running away from their target."
Traders were also closely watching the price movements in zinc, which marched up to hit a high of $1,538 on Wednesday, the highest level since a price crash last week.
At 0520 GMT, three-month price was not quoted. It finished the Wednesday kerb at $1,528, up $30 from the previous close.
"Weaker prices of the last few days triggered steady consumer interest. On top of that it's still unsure whether China has covered all its short positions," said one trader.
Another trader said: "I don't think they have as many short positions left as many seem to believe. The price should stay at these high levels for a while and then start sinking."
